opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what's exciting is that for the past several years, essentially every large language model has been built on the same basic recipe: autoregressive generation, predicting one token at a time, left to right. It's worked incredibly well, but it's a choice, not a law of nature. And it comes with some real limitations.

The most obvious one is speed. If you generate one token at a time, the cost of producing an answer scales with its length, and you're doing these sequential forward passes that don't make great use of modern GPUs, which are built for massive parallelism. Diffusion models work differently. You start from a noisy or fully masked sequence and refine the whole thing in parallel over a number of steps. So you can produce many tokens at once, and that gives you a very different speed-quality tradeoff. We've seen this play out in images and video, where diffusion became the dominant paradigm, and for a long time people assumed it just wouldn't transfer to discrete data like text. Part of what's exciting is that it turns out it does, once you get the modeling right.

But it's not only about speed. There's something conceptually appealing about a model that can revise its own output. An autoregressive model commits to a token and then has to live with it; if it makes a mistake early, it can only build on that mistake. A diffusion model looks at the entire sequence at every step and can go back and fix things. That's closer to how people actually write, especially for things like code, where you sketch the structure, fill in pieces, and go back and edit. It also gives you more natural control: infilling, editing, conditioning on constraints at arbitrary positions, not just a prefix.

And from a research perspective, it opens up a lot of questions we haven't fully answered: how these models scale, how to do reasoning and reinforcement learning with them, how to make inference adaptive so you spend more compute on harder parts. When a field has converged on one architecture for a long time, revisiting a basic assumption like the generation order is where I think a lot of interesting progress can come from.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that I think we've been treating autoregressive generation as if it were the only way to build a language model, when really it's just one point in a much larger design space. Diffusion opens up a different corner of that space, and it has properties that I think matter a lot in practice.

The first thing is speed. Autoregressive models produce one token at a time, left to right, and every token requires another full forward pass through the network. That's fundamentally sequential, and it's why inference is expensive and latency is hard to drive down. Diffusion models work differently. You start from noise, or in the discrete case from a fully masked sequence, and you refine the whole thing in parallel over a series of steps. So instead of your cost scaling with the number of tokens, it scales with the number of refinement steps, and you can trade that off against quality in a way you really can't with a transformer decoding left to right. We've seen that you can get many times the throughput for comparable quality, and that gap matters enormously once you're thinking about agentic workloads where a model might generate hundreds of thousands of tokens to solve one task.

The second thing is that diffusion gives you a kind of bidirectional, global view of the sequence during generation. An autoregressive model has to commit to each token before it knows what comes later. If it makes a mistake early, there's no going back, and that's part of why you see hallucinations and inconsistencies compound over long outputs. A diffusion model can revisit any part of the sequence at any step. It can plan, it can fix things, it can enforce constraints like "this output must have exactly this structure" or "this code must compile" in a much more natural way. Tasks like infilling and editing, which are awkward for left-to-right models, are just native to this framework.

And the third reason, honestly, is that it worked in images and it worked in audio and video, and for a long time people assumed it just wouldn't work for text because text is discrete. My group spent years on the foundations of discrete diffusion, score entropy, masked diffusion, and the lesson was that the gap between diffusion and autoregressive models on language was not a fundamental one. It was an engineering and scaling gap. Once we started scaling these things up, the quality came along, and now we have a real alternative with a different and arguably better set of tradeoffs.

So the reason I'm excited is that this isn't a marginal improvement on the existing paradigm. It's a different paradigm, and the economics of inference, the controllability, the ability to reason over the whole output at once, all point in a direction that I think the field is going to care about a lot more as models move from chat into actually doing work.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that they give us a different way to think about generating language. With an autoregressive model, you generate one token at a time, from left to right. That’s a very natural approach, and it works incredibly well, but it’s not the only way to do it.

With diffusion, you can start with a rough candidate and iteratively refine it. The model can work on different parts of a sequence, taking into account context on both sides. That’s appealing for things like filling in missing text or generating something subject to constraints, where you don’t necessarily want to commit to the beginning before you’ve figured out the end.

There’s also an interesting computational opportunity. Sequential token generation is a bottleneck, so being able to update many tokens in parallel could be valuable. Of course, diffusion requires multiple refinement steps, so whether you actually gain speed depends on how you design the model and the sampler.

I think the exciting research question is whether we can turn that flexibility into better quality, better control, or more efficient generation. We’ve seen how powerful diffusion can be for images. Language has different challenges because it’s discrete, but that makes it a really interesting space to explore.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find exciting is that they give us a different way to think about generating language. With an autoregressive model, you commit to one token at a time, going from left to right. With diffusion, you can start with a rough candidate and iteratively refine it. You can revise different parts of the sequence, and potentially generate many tokens in parallel.

That opens up some interesting possibilities. If you’re writing code, for example, you might know what needs to go at the beginning and at the end, and you want to fill in the middle. Or you might want to revise an answer while satisfying some constraints. Those tasks fit naturally with this idea of iterative refinement.

Of course, parallel generation doesn’t automatically make the whole process faster—you have to account for the refinement steps. But I think exploring that tradeoff, and whether a different generation process can give us new capabilities, makes this a very exciting research direction.
